newsitem.title: USA: US Midwest growth gauge of Fed's tolerance - sources.
newsitem.headline: US Midwest growth gauge of Fed's tolerance - sources.

text.p: Federal Reserve bank presidents in the booming Midwest are pushing for higher interest rates, signaling the type of growth and unemployment rates the Fed would deem inflationary at the national level, Fed sources said in interviews conducted Thursday and Friday.
"The Midwest presidents all have in their districts the kind of growth that, if it were at the national level, would have warranted a tightening a long time ago," one Fed source told Reuters.
"Some banks have already submitted requests for a discount rate hike. It's essentially symbolic, but it reflects the conditions in some districts," the source added.

At least one of the requests for a discount rate hike submitted to the Fed Board came from a bank that requested a discount rate cut in January when the Fed last moved to ease credit, the sources said.
The Midwest, which if it were a nation would boast the fourth largest economy in the world, is enjoying a growth rate about one percentage point above the 1996 U.S. 3.0-percent average.
The region's unemployment rate has recently been running about one percentage point below the national average.

One of the sources noted all five Midwest Fed banks -- Chicago, Cleveland, Kansas City, Minneapolis and St. Louis -- have "reported tight labor markets, some shortage of entry-level or skilled workers, and some wage acceleration."
Citing inflationary risks, Minneapolis Fed President Gary Stern dissented in favor of a rate hike at the July 2-3 Federal Open Market Committee meeting that kept rates steady.

"It's Minneapolis' Beige Book that coined the expression 'discouraged employers'," the first source pointed out, referring to the district's report about companies that have given up hope of finding skilled workers.
The Midwest has outperformed the U.S. economy throughout the current expansion cycle, resulting in a heightened regional focus on tight labor markets and inflation risks.

Another Midwest central banker, Cleveland Fed President Jerry Jordan, dissented in favor of a greater rate hike on March 22, 1994, when the Fed launched its preemptive tightening cycle with small 25-basis-point moves.

Jordan is a voting FOMC member again this year, following FOMC rules which allow four of the 11 banks to vote on a rotating basis each year. The 12th bank, New York, whose president is the FOMC vice-chairman, has a permanent vote.
Kansas City Fed President Thomas Hoenig also dissented against easing in July 1995.
The sources said the bank presidents, who have equal opportunity to air their views at FOMC gatherings regardless of their voting status, are almost evenly divided about the need to raise rates.
Sharing the Midwest bankers' concerns are anti-inflation hawks such as Richmond Fed President Alfred Broaddus who dissented three times in 1994 in favor of a tighter policy.
"The fact is monetary policy is not conducted for a region, but for the nation," the first source said, noting that the mid-Atlantic region and the West Coast are not enjoying above-trend growth.
"The Fed is anti-inflation as opposed to anti-growth," the source further stressed.
Another Fed source said central bank governors are "willing" to examine more economic data before making a decision on rates.
That source said requests for a discount rate hike would not, by themselves, sway the central bank into action because such a request is submitted to a vote among Fed governors.
"The governors would be reluctant to dissent on a discount rate vote," the source added.
